questions.question: Which practice helps improve river water quality? a). Dumping waste b). Wastewater treatment c). Channel narrowing d). Over-extraction of water / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Fecal Indicator Bacteria (FIB) : Escherichia coli , fecal coliforms, and intestinal enterococci are used to indicate the
  • presence of pathogens. Pathogenic Microorganisms: Detection of specific harmful organisms like Salmonella, Vibrio
  • cholerae, and protozoa. Total Viable Count (TVC): Measures the overall bacterial population, indicating organic
  • pollution levels.
  • Assessment Methodologies
  • Sample Collection: Aseptically collecting water in sterile containers. Serial Dilution: Tenfold dilution (e.g., in Ringers
  • solution) to enable colony counting. Membrane Filtration Technique: Passing water through a filter, then incubating
  • on selective media. Most Probable Number (MPN) : A statistical method to estimate the number of viable bacteria.
  • Incubation: Culturing samples (commonly 22°C and 37°C) to isolate specific bacteria.
  • Factors Affecting Microbiological Quality
  • Pollution Sources : Urban wastewater, industrial waste, agricultural runoff, and livestock waste increase microbial
  • loads. Environmental Factors : Rainfall, water temperature, flow rate, and season affect bacterial survival. Self-
  • purification: Natural ability of t he river to reduce contaminants
  • Impacts of contamination : High concentrations of E. coli (>2000 MPN/100ml) indicate severe contamination,
  • rendering water unsafe for recreational use. Contaminated water can cause illnesses like cholera, giardiasis, and
  • dysentery, especially in developing regions. Routine monitoring is essential for identifying pathogens and pro tecting
  • public health.

• Lower Course (Gentle Slope): Very gentle slope near the mouth. Characterized by deposition, resulting in floodplains
  • and deltas.
  • Key Concepts in Longitudinal Profiles
  • Graded Profile: A smoothed, balanced profile where energy allows for the transport of sediment load.
  • Base Level: The lowest point a river can erode to, usually sea level, though lakes can be local, temporary base levels.
  • Knickpoint: A sharp change in the slope of the profile (e.g., a waterfall or steep rapid), often signaling a previous
  • change in sea level or geological uplift.
  • Factors Influencing the Profile
  • Erosion and Deposition: The key processes that shape the profile, with steeper parts favoring erosion and flatter parts
  • favoring deposition.
  • Base Level Changes: A drop in sea level can create more steepening, while a rise in sea level can lead to increased
  • deposition.
  • Geological Structure: Hard and soft rocks can cause unevenness, known as an ungraded profile, which will erode into
  • a smoother shape over time.

questions.question: Describe the Meenachil River MRRM model and its objectives. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the Meenachil River MRRM model and its objectives. [U] / [CO2]
  • The Meenachil River & Rain Monitoring Network (MRRM) is a community -driven initiative in Kerala, using ~170+
  • rain gauges to monitor water levels and manage flood risks from Vagamon to Vembanad Lake. Key hydrological models
  • applied to the basin include SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) for water quality and HEC -HMS for rainfall-
  • runoff simulation.
  • Key Aspects of Meenachil River Modeling & Monitoring:
  • MRRM Network (Community Monitoring): Initiated in 2019, this network involves local volunteers (e.g., Meenachil
  • River Protection Council) monitoring river gauges at locations like Erattupetta, Teekoy, and Kidangoor to provide real-
  • time data.
  • Hydrological Models Used : SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool): Applied to simulate streamflow, calibrate
  • water quality, and analyze sediment/nutrient loads in the Meenachil River Basin (MRB).
  • HEC-HMS (Hydrologic Modeling System): Used to model flood scenarios in the sub-basin, achieving high accuracy
  • (NSE > 0.7) in predicting peak flows.
  • Flood Management & Data: These models, along with the MRRM network data, are crucial for hazard mapping, flood
  • forecasting, and operating local infrastructure like the Kanakkankadavu shutters to prevent i nundation in agricultural
  • areas. The river, spanning approximately 78 km, requires intense monitoring due to its flash flood susceptibility within
  • the tropical humid zone of the Western Ghats.

questions.question: Describe the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and its objectives. / [CO3]

• Describe the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and its objectives. [U] / [CO3]
  • The Convention on Biological Diversity (Biodiversity Convention or CBD) entered into force in December 1993, and
  • has been ratified by almost 200 nations. The CBD is a 'Rio Convention' – it is one of three Conventions adopted at the
  • "Earth Summit" (the Conference on Environment and Development), held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil in 1992. The other
  • two Conventions adopted were the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change ), and the Convention to Combat
  • Desertification.
  • As the first global treaty to provide a legal framework for biodiversity conservation, the Convention established three
  • main goals: 1) the conservation of biological diversity 2) the sustainable use of its components3) fair and equitable
  • sharing of the benefits arising from the use of genetic resources.
  • Contracting Parties are required to create and enforce national strategies and action plans to conserve, protect and
  • enhance biological diversity. They are also required to undertake action to implement the thematic work programmes
  • on ecosystems and a rang e of cross -cutting issues which have been established to take forward the provisions of the
  • Convention.
  • In January 2000 the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety was adopted to supplement the provisions of the Convention.
  • This Agreement, which came into force in September 2003, aims to ensure the safe handling, transport and use of living
  • modified organisms (LMOs), resulting from modern Biotechnology.
  • Subsequently, the Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits
  • Arising from their Utilization to the Convention on Biological Diversity was adopted on 29 October 2010 and entered
  • into force on 12 October 2014 (ratified by UK 22 May 2016). The Nagoya Protocol aims to share the benefits arising

questions.question: Classify mineral substrates in the riverbed based on partied size. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Classify mineral substrates in the riverbed based on partied size. [U] / [CO1]
  • Mineral substrates in riverbeds are classified based on particle size into categories ranging from fine mud to large
  • boulders and bedrock. Their distribution is driven by flow velocity, transport capacity and geological sources. Generally
  • riverbeds exhibit a downstream fining trend and coarser particles are found in upstream areas.
  • Based on common geological and ecological classifications riverbed substrates are divided into:
  • -Bedrock (>512 mm): Solid rock in the channel base – typical in high gradient steep streams
  • -Boulder (256-512 mm): Large heavy rocks, often found in mountain streams
  • -Cobble (64-256 mm): Smaller than boulders, provide stable and heterogeneous habitats
  • -Gravel (2-64 mm): Further divided into coarse gravel (16-64mm) and fine gravel (2 -16mm). Generally gravel is the
  • key substrate for fish spawning.
  • -Sand (0.06-2mm): Divided into coarse (0.5 – 2mm) and fine (0.06 -0.5 mm) sand. Often fills the gaps between larger
  • stable substrates or forms mobile beds in lower gradient sections.
  • -Silt/Mud (0.06mm): Very fine particles that usually accumulate in low velocity areas. (The exact measurements used
  • in Wentworth Scale may also be considered.)

questions.question: Describe the major physical parameters used in river assessment. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the major physical parameters used in river assessment. [U] / [CO2]
  • Major physical parameters to assess a river include channel morphology (width, depth, slope), discharge (flow volume),
  • velocity, turbidity, water temperature, and total suspended/dissolved solids (TSS/TDS). These parameters define the
  • river's energy, ability to transport sediment, and health, indicating habitat quality and identifying pollution sources.
  • Key Physical Assessment Parameters
  • Channel Morphology: Width and Depth: Key in determining the cross -sectional area and the hydraulic capacity.
  • Gradient (Slope): Determines the energy, speed, and erosion type (vertical or lateral). Channel Profile: Longitudinal
  • changes from source (steep) to mouth (gentle) and cross -sections. Pools and Riffles: Shallow areas (riffles) and deep
  • pools indicate habitat diversity.
  • Hydraulic Features: Discharge (Q): Total volume of water passing a point over time, crucial for flood assessment.
  • Velocity: Speed of flow, often measured at different depths and locations. Thalweg: The deepest part of the channel,
  • marking the line of fastest flow.
  • Water Physical Properties: Temperature: Influences chemical and biological processes, influenced by climate and
  • shading. Turbidity: A measure of water clarity, affected by suspended particles. Total Suspended Solids (TSS) &
  • Total Dissolved Solids (TDS): Indicate sediment loading and ionic concentration, respectively. Colour and
  • Odour: Basic sensory parameters indicating pollution or sedimentation issues.
  • Geomorphological Features: Meanders/Curvature: Bends in the river that indicate erosion on the outer bank and
  • deposition on the inner bank. Sediment Type: Substrate composition (e.g., sand, gravel, rocks) in the riverbed.

questions.question: Describe Strahler stream order method. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe Strahler stream order method. [U] / [CO1]
  • Strahler stream ordering is a method for classifying streams based on hierarchical tributaries. The smallest,
  • unbranched, permanent streams are designated as 1st order. When two streams of the same order (N) join, they form a
  • higher order stream (N+1). Merging different orders, retains the higher orders.
  • Key Principles: 1st Order: Headwater streams with no tributaries. Increases by 1: Only when two streams of the
  • same order meet. (1+1=2, 2+2=3)
  • Different Orders: If a 1st order stream joins a 2nd order stream, the channel remains 2nd order. This method is used to
  • characterize watershed morphology, including drainage density, stream frequency and bifurcation ratio. It helps to
  • identify headwaters (1 to 3 orders), intermediate streams (4 to 6 orders) and larger river (7+). Often used to define
  • legal, environmental or regulating restrictions for building dams or managing water rights.

questions.question: Describe the Pen culture practices carried out in Kerala state. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the Pen culture practices carried out in Kerala state. [U] / [CO5]
  • Pen culture in Kerala is primarily utilized as a climate-resilient technology for rearing fish fry to fingerlings in reservoirs,
  • wetlands, and waterlogged areas, rather than just in the main flowing rivers themselves. This technique involves fencing
  • shallow parts of the water body using bamboo poles and HDPE nets to allow for natural food availability while
  • protecting the fish.
  • Key pen culture practices in Kerala include:
  • Seed Rearing (Nursery Management): Primarily used for raising fry to advanced fingerlings before releasing them
  • into the larger water body (reservoir/wetland), which ensures higher survival rates.
  • Species Cultivated: Key species include Indian Major Carps (Catla, Rohu, Mrigal), Grass Carp , and Pearlspot
  • (Etroplus suratensis) Integrated Systems: Pen culture is often integrated with clam farming in brackish water wetlands,
  • where nets hold the clams in place during cultivation. Site Management: HDPE pens are installed in shallow regions
  • of water bodies like the Vazhani and Malampuzha reservoirs . Flood Mitigation: It has been identified as a reliable
  • method to withstand environmental crises, such as the 2018 flood, by protecting fish stock, as seen in studies of Black
  • clam culture. These initiatives are often spearheaded by the Department of Fisheries and the Kerala State Co-operative
  • Federation for Fisheries. Development (Matsyafed) as part of inland fish production enhancement, often in collaboration
  • with research institutes like ICAR-CIFRI and CMFRI.

questions.question: What is longitudinal profile of a river ? Give its key characteristics. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4, CO5] [4x8 = 32]
questions.solution_html:
• What is longitudinal profile of a river? Give its key characteristics. [U] / [CO1]
  • A longitudinal profile is a graph showin
  • g the elevation changes of a riverbed
  • along its entire course, from the source (highest elevation) to the mouth (lowest elevation/base level). It typically forms
  • a smooth concave curve, being steep in the upper course and flattening out towards the lower c ourse, representing a
  • balance between erosion and deposition.
  • Characteristics of a River Profile
  • Concave Shape : The profile is generally concave upward, representing a steady state of equilibrium where a river
  • transports its sediment load efficiently.
  • Upper Course (Steep Slope) : Located near the source in high -relief areas. Characterized by vertical erosion, steep
  • gradients, fast flow, and features like rapids and waterfalls.
  • Middle Course (Moderate Slope) : Gradient decreases, resulting in less vertical erosion and more lateral
  • erosion/transportation.
